documents: Bissbort, Lynn, Becker & Chakraborty (2022), Hydrogen diffusion in clinopyroxene at low temperatures (195°C–400°C) and consequences for subsurface processes, G-Cubed 23, e2022GC010520 (published PDF, 18 pages)
pages_convention: printed journal pages (article pages 'n of 18', identical to PDF pages counted from 1)

entry.evidence: These quantities are known only by extrapolation of high temperature data

steps.action: Pose whether surface-collected NAM hydrogen contents record mantle values, and state that answering this needs hydrogen diffusion rates at low temperatures (<<600°C), known only by extrapolation.
steps.quote: a legitimate question that remains is whether hydrogen concentrations that are measured in NAMs collected on Earth's surface really represent the original H contents

steps.action: Combine hydrogen ion implantation with Nuclear Resonance Reaction Analysis (NRRA) into a method for measuring low-temperature H diffusion on nanometre-scale profiles.
steps.quote: We combined two experimental methods, ion implantation and Nuclear Resonance Reaction Analysis (NRRA), to develop a method

steps.action: Characterize the gem diopside starting material by electron microprobe (composition, Fe3+ by Droop) and Laue orientation, then cut slabs perpendicular to [001] and polish them.
steps.quote: The crystallographic orientation was verified by Laue analysis

steps.action: Simulate implantation profiles with SRIM to choose a beam energy that places the H peak (~650 nm) far from surface contamination but within NRRA depth range; omit chemical polishing because diffusion is not studied near the surface.
steps.quote: Concentration profiles were simulated using the software SRIM (Ziegler et al., 2010) prior to the actual implantation

steps.action: Implant H at 60 keV (fluence 1.48e16 at/cm2) and anneal the samples at 195, 270 and 400°C in a gas-mixing furnace flushed with CO2, with quench.
steps.quote: The furnace was flushed with 100 vol% CO2 to establish non-oxidizing conditions during experiments

steps.action: Measure H depth profiles by NRRA before (initial condition) and after each anneal in the same sample, including a three-step time series at 270°C.
steps.quote: Hydrogen concentration depth profiles were obtained by NRRA in each sample after implantation and before diffusion experiments

steps.action: Fit an explicit finite-difference solution of Fick's second law, starting from the measured initial profile, to each annealed profile by misfit minimization to obtain D (Table 1).
steps.quote: D values were constrained by minimizing the misfit (σfit) between each measured concentration

steps.action: Check the method with the 270°C time series in one sample: D values stay nearly constant (scatter ~0.24 log units) over 40–220 min.
steps.quote: It was also used to assess the suitability of our method for obtaining diffusion coefficients

steps.action: Fit an Arrhenius relation to the diffusion coefficients from 195–400°C: D = 5.47e-8 exp(-115.6 kJ/mol/RT) m2/s.
steps.quote: Diffusion rates that were determined in our experiments describe an Arrhenius relation

steps.action: Assemble the published high-temperature (≥600°C) Arrhenius laws for clinopyroxene (Ingrin 1995, Hercule & Ingrin 1999, Woods 2000, Sundvall 2009, Ferriss 2016) and extrapolate them to 195–400°C as the expected range (Figure 4).
steps.quote: a comparison of our results with those of other studies in clinopyroxene is restricted to higher temperatures (≥600°C)

steps.action: Compare the low-temperature D values with the extrapolations: they fall within the Fe-bearing diopside range, agree closely with Kunlun diopside (Ferriss 2016) and lie far above the Fe-free trend.
steps.quote: Our results lay well within the range that is constrained by extrapolation of Arrhenius relationships from high temperature experiments

steps.action: Revise the Fe-content control on H diffusivity: agreement with a much lower-Fe diopside implies a more complex composition–diffusivity relation.
steps.quote: also indicates a more complex composition-diffusivity relationship

steps.action: Check two premises of the implantation method: radiation damage (it would produce asymmetric profile evolution, which is not observed) and H speciation (a change would make D vary with time, but the time series is constant; OH bonding is cited from olivine IR work).
steps.quote: This was not observed in our diffusion profiles (Figure 2).

steps.action: Keep the claim that fast H diffusion in clinopyroxene continues to low temperatures along the extrapolated Arrhenius behaviour.
steps.quote: it is evident that the high diffusivity of hydrogen (compared to other elements) in clinopyroxene extends continuously toward low temperatures

steps.action: Build a non-isothermal diffusion model of 0.5–2 mm crystals ascending from 600 to 100°C along continental and oceanic geotherms at 0.1–1000°C/yr, with solubility-controlled boundary concentrations from a C-saturated C-O-H fluid at QMF (Appendix A).
steps.quote: We have developed a model that simulates diffusion of hydrogen in clinopyroxene during its ascent

steps.action: Vary the boundary condition (fixed 0 ppm instead of variable solubility) for 1 mm crystals at 100°C/yr: re-equilibration is much stronger and profile shapes differ.
steps.quote: we changed the boundaries to a fixed low concentration (=0 wt. ppm) right from the start of diffusion process

steps.action: Fit re-equilibration as a function of crystal size and cooling rate for each geotherm (Equation 5, Levenberg–Marquardt fits in Appendix B) and map it (Figure 7).
steps.quote: The dependence of re-equilibration on crystal size and cooling rate follows a systematic behavior that can be described by Equation 5

steps.action: Model isothermal dwelling at 300°C (serpentinization) for a 2 mm crystal with several fixed boundary concentrations over 2,000 and 20,000 years (Figure 9).
steps.quote: Results from modeling hydrogen diffusion in clinopyroxene at 300°C illustrate the development of the hydrogen distribution at temperatures associated with serpentinization

steps.action: Set the model maps against natural cases: kimberlite-borne xenoliths (Bell & Rossman 1992; Peslier & Bizimis 2015) likely preserve mantle H, volcanic profiles freeze in at high temperature, and slow cooling or serpentinization can erase the signal.
steps.quote: mantle xenoliths that were transported to the surface in a kimberlitic magma probably preserved the original hydrogen content

steps.action: Note slowly cooled rocks with H-rich clinopyroxene that sit uneasily with the model, and propose untested explanations (composition, shielding by other phases, other diffusion mechanisms) for future work.
steps.quote: These may be effects of composition of the clinopyroxenes, shielding by other phases

steps.action: Conclude on the method, the Arrhenius law, the validity of extrapolation, and the size and cooling-rate thresholds for preserving mantle H contents.
steps.quote: thus erasing the hydrogen content equilibrated at mantle depths.

tree.answer: Diffusive H loss or gain in clinopyroxene; rates known only above 600°C
No; D is inferred from NRRA profiles through a forward diffusion model
Estimate low-temperature D and test whether high-temperature extrapolation holds
No explicit rivals; implicitly, extrapolation holds or fails at low temperature
Extrapolated literature Arrhenius laws give an expected D range
Set in the lab: anneals at 195, 270 and 400°C in CO2
Time-series constancy, damage and speciation checks; boundary-condition sensitivity in the model
Kept: D lies within the extrapolated range; fast diffusion extends to low temperature

end.claim: Hydrogen diffusion in natural diopsidic clinopyroxene at 195–400°C follows D = 5.47(±13.98)e-8 exp(-115.6(±11.5) kJ/mol/RT) m2/s, within the range extrapolated from high-temperature experiments, so fast H diffusion extends to low temperatures.

decisive_move.sentence: Combining ion implantation with non-destructive NRRA depth profiling made nanometre-scale diffusion measurable at 195–400°C, which conventional dehydration and FTIR approaches could not reach.

gates.evidence: The open question of whether high-temperature extrapolation holds set the low temperature range, but no hypothesis with stated rivals directed the experiments (p. 2). The low-temperature D values could have fallen outside the extrapolated Arrhenius range (p. 7, Figure 4), although that range is broad. Nothing is reported as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Nuclear Resonance Reaction Analysis, 1H(15N,αγ)12C, with NaI(Tl) gamma detection
Hydrogen ion implantation at a 500 kV accelerator (duoplasmatron source) to create concentration gradients
Implantation damage of light versus heavy ions (Zhang et al. 2009)
Explicit finite-difference solution of Fick's second law; Levenberg–Marquardt nonlinear least squares (MATLAB)

novelty_claims.quote: Diffusion rates of hydrogen in clinopyroxene in the low temperature range (195°C–400°C) were quantified for the first time
we were able to resolve the outstanding issue whether diffusion rates can be extrapolated from high temperatures [...]
[...] of diffusion coefficients for hydrogen in NAMs was possible only at high temperatures (>600°C) up to now.

limits: No peer-review file was supplied (the acknowledgements thank J. Hermann and an anonymous reviewer), so no review sequence is coded. The dataset is five anneals on one crystal composition: one each at 195 and 400°C and three at 270°C. Orientation is only [001]. fO2 is not controlled. The pre-exponential uncertainty exceeds its value, and the time-series scatter is larger than the propagated errors (Figure 3). The H bonding state is assumed from olivine IR work (cited, not performed here). The fracture-affected 400°C profile is shown, but how those points were handled in the fit is not stated (inference). The comparison with independent high-temperature studies is coded as a replication performed here, because the paper carries out the comparison, although the independent data are others' (coder judgement). Sub-claims at other statuses: the validity of extrapolation to low temperature is best_explanation (consistency with a broad extrapolated range, stated as 'prove' on p. 14); the re-equilibration maps and Equation 5 are regularity_in_range, holding only for a C-saturated C-O-H fluid at QMF along the two illustrative geotherms (p. 12); preservation of mantle H in kimberlite-borne xenoliths is best_explanation (p. 12). The geological application steps are model outputs; no natural profiles are fitted. Composition is none_fits: a problem-driven, capability-enabled estimation compared with extrapolated literature expectations, with no stated rivals and no crucial test.

disagreements.target: Ferriss et al. (2016): H diffusivity in clinopyroxene increases with Fe content
disagreements.support: The XFe = 0.102 diopside agrees with the extrapolated law for Kunlun diopside (XFe = 0.025), which implies that Fe content alone does not control diffusivity.
disagreements.quote: also indicates a more complex composition-diffusivity relationship

disagreements.target: Interpretation that H contents of NAMs in mantle xenoliths record a mantle source (Bell & Rossman 1992)
disagreements.support: Model maps support preservation for fast kimberlite ascent but show erasure under slow cooling or serpentinization-temperature dwelling.
disagreements.quote: slow cooling or dwelling at temperatures that are typical for serpentinization (∼300°C, Guillot et al., 2015) can erase a mantle signature

disagreements.target: Ascent-rate modeling that assumes a large fixed dehydration gradient (0 ppm boundary) from the start
disagreements.support: A comparison of the 0 ppm boundary with variable solubility-controlled boundaries in the 1 mm models shows the simplified approach overestimates cooling rates by about an order of magnitude.
disagreements.quote: produces overestimates on the order of an order of magnitude or so in cooling rates

disagreements.target: Slowly cooled rocks with H-rich clinopyroxene (Katayama et al. 2006; Konzett et al. 2008; Urann et al. 2022)
disagreements.support: The paper notes these observations sit uneasily with its fast-diffusion results and offers untested explanations, deferring them to future work.
